description: I am a person who enjoys space science and is looking forward to working on the challenge of identifying analog sites that would help scientists achieve many goals.
summary: Our project investigates three terrestrial analogs to solve key astrobiological and engineering challenges for future Mars and Artemis lunar missions. First, we examine Spotted Lake in Canada, whose concentrated magnesium and sodium sulfate brines mirror ancient Martian paleolakes. Studying how extremophiles survive and leave biosignatures in these salt-rich pools informs how rovers search for past Martian life. Second, we explore Antarctica’s subglacial Lake Vostok to address the scientific debate over liquid water and potential habitats beneath Mars' polar ice caps. Analyzing how microbes persist in dark, isolated subglacial waters helps scientists evaluate subsurface Martian habitability. Finally, we examine Hawaii's volcanic terrains and lava tubes—specifically Mauna Ulu—as an analog for a permanent Artemis lunar base. Natural basaltic lava tubes provide thick overhead shielding against cosmic radiation and micrometeorites while allowing teams to test subterranean mapping and habitat protocols. Together, these analogs bridge Earth-based fieldwork with off-world exploration, guiding both the search for extraterrestrial life on Mars and safe human settlement on the Moon.
details:
Overview & How It Works

Our project presents a comparative planetary analog framework that uses extreme environments on Earth to solve key astrobiological and engineering challenges for future Mars and Artemis lunar missions. By analyzing verified geological and environmental data across three distinct terrestrial sites, we demonstrate how Earth-based fieldwork informs off-world exploration and human settlement:

1. Spotted Lake (British Columbia, Canada) – Mars Brine & Paleolake Analog: Examines how concentrated magnesium and sodium sulfate brines mirror ancient evaporating Martian lakes, helping astrobiologists understand how extremophiles survive and leave biosignatures in hyper-saline environments.

2. Lake Vostok (Antarctica) – Mars Subglacial Habitability Analog: Addresses the scientific debate over liquid water on Mars by studying how microbial life persists in dark, high-pressure subglacial water beneath thick ice sheets—a direct parallel to potential subsurface reservoirs beneath Mars' polar ice caps.

3. Mauna Ulu & Hawaiian Lava Tubes (Hawaiʻi, USA) – Artemis Lunar Base Analog: Evaluates young basaltic lava tubes on Kīlauea as natural subterranean shelters for a permanent Moon base. These hollow volcanic conduits offer thick rock overhead shielding against cosmic radiation and micrometeorites while allowing teams to test subterranean mapping, LiDAR, ground-penetrating radar (GPR), and skylight entry protocols.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Testing rover instruments, biosignature detection methods, and habitat protocols on Earth reduces mission risk and cost before launching hardware to the Moon or Mars. Our comparative presentation provides an accessible, scientifically grounded guide showing how terrestrial analogs directly support both the search for extraterrestrial life and safe, sustainable human habitation under the Artemis program.

Tools & Development

Research & Data Sources: Official peer-reviewed publications and planetary analog databases from NASA Science, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), and the National Park Service (NPS).

Software & Design: Microsoft PowerPoint for presentation design, visual comparisons, and structured educational storytelling.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered

Rather than focusing on a single planet or discipline, we creatively bridged astrobiology (searching for life on Mars) and planetary engineering (building permanent human habitats on the Moon) into one cohesive framework. For each analog, our team carefully weighed both its scientific strengths (geological accuracy, radiation shielding, extremophile preservation) and its operational weaknesses (navigating sharp volcanic glass, total darkness, and extreme cold) to ensure realistic, balanced mission planning.
